passages.t: Ariel besieged, and enemies like a dream
passages.happening:
“Woe to you, O Ariel, the city of Ariel where David camped!” (verse 1). Let the festivals go round year after year. God will bring distress on Ariel; there will be mourning, and she will be like an altar hearth before him (verse 2). He will camp around her and set up siege works (verse 3). She will be brought low and speak from the dust, her voice like a ghost's whisper from the ground (verse 4).

But suddenly her many foes will be like fine dust and blowing chaff (verse 5). The LORD of Hosts will come with thunder, earthquake, storm and fire (verse 6). All the nations fighting against Ariel ‘will be like a dream, like a vision in the night’ (verse 7), like a hungry man who dreams he is eating and wakes up still hungry, or a thirsty man who dreams of drinking and wakes up parched. ‘So will it be for all the many nations who go to battle against Mount Zion’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The second woe of this section turns fully to Jerusalem. Ariel is a name for Jerusalem, the city where David camped, since David captured Jerusalem and made it his capital. The word ariel also seems to mean an altar hearth, the top of the altar where offerings burned, which is why verse 2 says the city will be like one.

The siege is usually connected with the Assyrian threat that reached its height in Sennacherib's campaign of 701 BC. Assyria overran the fortified cities of Judah and threatened Jerusalem, but the city was not taken, and the book records that the Assyrian army was struck down in a single night. Verses 5 to 8 read like a preview of that sudden reversal: the attackers who seem so solid vanish like a dream at waking.

The first hearers kept their festivals year after year, as if nothing were wrong. Isaiah tells them God himself will bring them low before he rescues them.
passages.later: Isaiah later tells how ‘the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians’ (Isaiah 37:36). A psalm says of the wicked, ‘Like one waking from a dream, so You, O Lord, awaken and despise their form’ (Psalm 73:20).
passages.asks: The enemies that seemed so solid vanished like a dream. Ask what fear in your life might be like that. And ask whether you are keeping up the festivals of faith while your heart is elsewhere, as Ariel did.

passages.t: Lips near, hearts far, and the clay and the potter
passages.happening:
‘Stop and be astonished; blind yourselves and be sightless; be drunk, but not with wine’ (verse 9). The LORD has poured out on them a spirit of deep sleep and shut the eyes of the prophets (verse 10). The whole vision is like a sealed scroll: one person cannot read it because it is sealed, another because he cannot read (verses 11-12).

The Lord says, ‘These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men’ (verse 13). So he will again astonish them with wonder upon wonder; ‘The wisdom of the wise will vanish’ (verse 14).

‘Woe to those who dig deep to hide their plans from the LORD’ (verse 15). They work in the dark and ask who sees them. They have turned things upside down, as if the potter were clay. Can the pot say of the potter that he did not make it, or that he has no understanding (verse 16)?
passages.hearers:
This half of the chapter exposes the deeper problem beneath Jerusalem's false refuge: a religion of routine that no longer knows God. They say the right words. Their hearts are elsewhere. Their worship is a set of human rules learned by rote.

The sealed scroll is a sharp picture. The learned say they cannot read it because it is sealed; the unlearned say they cannot read. Either way, God's word goes unheard.

Verse 15 reflects the politics of Hezekiah's court, where officials were planning alliances in secret, probably the negotiations with Egypt that chapters 30 and 31 condemn openly. Isaiah's complaint was not only that the plans were unwise, but that they were hidden from God and from his prophet. The pot cannot hide from the potter.
passages.later: Jesus quoted verse 13 against those who set aside God's command for their own traditions: ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me’ (Matthew 15:8). Paul quotes verse 14: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise’ (1 Corinthians 1:19). And Jeremiah hears God say, ‘Just like clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in My hand’ (Jeremiah 18:6).
passages.hard:
If the LORD pours out a spirit of deep sleep on the people (verse 10), how can they be blamed for not seeing?

This is the same difficulty raised by Isaiah's commission in 6:9-10. The text holds two things together. The people have already closed their own eyes: verse 9 tells them to blind themselves. And God confirms the blindness they have chosen as a judgment. Many interpreters call this judicial hardening, God handing people over to what they persistently prefer, as Paul describes in Romans 1.

The chapter does not leave it there. The same God who shuts eyes promises to open them (verse 18) and to bring the wayward to understanding (verse 24). Hardening in Isaiah serves a larger purpose of healing.

Verse 13 was spoken by a prophet of Judah to his own people's leaders, and Jesus used it as Isaiah did, as a warning about empty religion. It is a warning for every community that worships, the church included. It is not a label for the Jewish people, then or now.
passages.asks: The people honored God with their lips while their hearts were far away. Ask whether your worship has become rules learned by rote. And ask what plans you are making in the dark, as if God could not see.

passages.t: The deaf will hear and the blind will see
passages.happening:
In a very short time, will not Lebanon become an orchard, and the orchard a forest (verse 17)? ‘On that day the deaf will hear the words of the scroll, and out of the deep darkness the eyes of the blind will see’ (verse 18). ‘The humble will increase their joy in the LORD, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel’ (verse 19).

The ruthless will vanish and the mockers disappear (verse 20), those who twist a man's words in court, trap the one who argues for justice at the gate, and deprive the innocent with false charges (verse 21).

So the LORD who redeemed Abraham says, ‘No longer will Jacob be ashamed and no more will his face grow pale’ (verse 22). When he sees his children, the work of God's hands, they will honor God's name and stand in awe of the God of Israel (verse 23). ‘Then the wayward in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will accept instruction’ (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The chapter turns from blindness to sight. The sealed scroll of verse 11 is now heard, even by the deaf. The poor and the humble rejoice, and the ruthless who corrupted the courts are gone.

The gate was where cases were judged. Those who trap the advocate at the gate are people who silence anyone who speaks for the innocent.

The promise of opened eyes and ears runs through the rest of the book, in chapters 32, 35 and 42. The first hearers, whose prophets had their eyes shut, were promised a day when even the blind would see.
passages.later: Isaiah repeats the promise: ‘Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped’ (Isaiah 35:5). And Jesus answered John's disciples, ‘The blind receive sight, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear’ (Matthew 11:5), in words drawn largely from Isaiah.
passages.asks: God promises that the wayward will come to understanding and the grumblers will accept teaching. Ask where you have been wayward or grumbling. And ask what you have been deaf to in God's word that you might hear again.
